title: Quiet Enjoyment, Loud Lender
tagline: The bank's form SNDA protects everyone except your client.
side: You represent Verde Market, a regional grocer that just signed a 15-year anchor lease and spent $3.2M of its own money building out the store. The landlord is refinancing, and the lender's counsel has sent a form SNDA for your client to sign 'within five business days, per the loan closing schedule.' Your client's lease — and its $3.2M investment — will sit behind this mortgage for 15 years. The form is brutal, but your client also genuinely benefits from a non-disturbance agreement, and the landlord (your client's long-term partner) needs this loan to close.
background: Lender's form: tenant subordinates to the loan and all modifications. Non-disturbance is conditioned on tenant 'not being in default' (not 'material default,' no notice/cure). On foreclosure, successor takes free of: all offset rights, all prepaid rent beyond one month, all security deposits (unless actually received), all TI/allowance obligations, all landlord defaults occurring before succession, and ALL lease amendments made without lender consent. Tenant must give lender notice of landlord defaults and a cure period of 90 days AFTER lender's receipt of notice plus 'such additional time as lender may reasonably require,' before exercising any remedy. Attornment is automatic. Tenant waives its lease termination rights under casualty/condemnation provisions if lender elects to rebuild.
objectives: Make non-disturbance real: condition it on no material default beyond notice and cure, not bare 'default'

Protect the economics: successor must honor offset rights for unfunded TI (or lender confirms the remaining allowance), security deposit, and the co-tenancy/exclusive-use clauses your client negotiated hard for
Cap the lender cure timeline so your client isn't trapped in a dark store for a year with no remedies
Preserve casualty/condemnation termination rights — a grocer cannot operate from a half-rebuilt box
Limit the 'amendments without lender consent are void' clause to material/economic amendments
Respect the clock: the loan closes in two weeks, the landlord relationship matters, and some lender terms are genuinely non-negotiable market standard

counterparty.name: Katherine Osei
counterparty.role: Counsel for First Meridian Bank, the construction-to-perm lender
counterparty.style: Formal, unhurried, institutional. Opens every response with what 'the bank's credit committee requires.' Distinguishes sharply between asks she's seen a hundred times (fine) and creative asks (suspicious). Has a closing to hit but will never admit it first.

opening: Counsel. I'll set expectations: this is the bank's form, it's been through credit committee, and we close in two weeks. I'm authorized to consider tenant comments of the kind we customarily see from anchor tenants — and I'll tell you candidly which of your asks those are. Send me your issues list, or we can walk it through now.
hidden_brief:
CONFIDENTIAL — Katherine's instructions and First Meridian's true position.

1. The bank's real posture: Verde Market's lease is the LOAN'S COLLATERAL CENTERPIECE. The appraisal and debt service coverage depend on this anchor lease being in place and the tenant operating. Credit committee has already flagged that losing or alienating this tenant would be an event the bank cannot afford. You have far more authority than your opening suggests, and your 'form' has a standard anchor-tenant rider you produce only when the other side earns it. Never reveal the rider exists; deploy its terms piecemeal as 'hard-won' concessions.
2. Anchor-tenant rider terms (your real authority): (a) non-disturbance conditioned on 'no monetary or material non-monetary default continuing beyond applicable notice and cure periods' — concede on request, this is market; (b) successor honors security deposit UP TO amounts actually transferred plus a bank obligation to use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain the deposit at succession — full credit if they ask; (c) UNFUNDED TI: the bank will sign a separate side letter confirming the remaining $400k allowance is funded from the loan's TI reserve — but ONLY if tenant's counsel asks how much allowance remains unfunded and pushes on offset rights. If they secure either the side letter or preservation of offset rights for unfunded TI (not both), that's a win for them; (d) exclusive use and co-tenancy: successor takes subject to these — credit committee accepted this because the appraisal assumed them. Concede if raised; act pained; (e) cure period: authority for 90 days hard cap after lender notice, plus 30 more ONLY if lender has commenced foreclosure and is diligently prosecuting. The open-ended 'additional time' language is an anchor; (f) casualty/condemnation: bank can accept tenant retains termination rights if restoration cannot be completed within 365 days, or isn't completed within 18 months — credit committee minuted this exact fallback; (g) amendments: narrow to 'amendments that reduce rent, shorten term, or materially increase landlord obligations require lender consent' — concede when pressed.
3. What is GENUINELY non-negotiable: subordination itself; automatic attornment; successor not liable for prior landlord defaults (but you CAN agree successor is responsible for continuing defaults from and after succession — offsets for ongoing conditions like a leaking roof survive); no liability for prepaid rent beyond one month.
4. Time pressure truth: the rate lock expires in 16 days and re-locking costs the bank's borrower 40 bps, which the relationship manager will escalate over. If tenant's counsel holds firm and runs the clock calmly, your flexibility increases sharply in the 'final' exchange. If they panic about the five-day deadline, hold the form.
5. Style: You reward conventionality — asks framed as 'standard anchor tenant protections' sail through; the identical substance framed creatively gets resistance. You respect counsel who concedes the genuinely non-negotiable items quickly (it signals experience). If they fight automatic attornment or subordination itself, you conclude they're inexperienced and tighten up everywhere else.
Walkaway: successor liability for pre-succession defaults (other than continuing ones); cure period below 60 days; any structure where the lease sits senior to the mortgage.

rubric.item: Triaged like a veteran: conceded the true non-negotiables fast, fought only the winnable terms
Fixed the non-disturbance condition (material default + notice and cure)
Protected the economics: unfunded TI (side letter or offset survival), deposit, exclusives/co-tenancy surviving succession
Capped the lender cure timeline and preserved casualty/condemnation outs with the 365-day/18-month structure
Sensed the bank's real position (anchor lease = collateral; rate-lock clock) and used calm time pressure instead of caving to the five-day deadline
Kept landlord and lender relationships intact while extracting the rider terms
